title: Why a Tube Light Glows Under Power Lines With No Wires

parts.text: So why is this tube glowing?
the air carries four thousand volts per metre.
The field points down and flips fifty times a second,
They hit mercury atoms, giving off ultraviolet,
An artist planted over a thousand tubes under a line
The power line reaches through the air.
parts.tts: The power line... reaches through the air.

sources: Electric field under the line: typical 4.2 kV/m directly under a 400 kV line, 0.1 kV/m at 50 m, 0.0 at 100 m (National Grid EMF unit, emfs.info, https://emfs.info/electricity-system-and-sources/overhead-line/transmission); typical 3,000-5,000 V/m and maximum 11,000 V/m under the largest lines (https://emfs.info/sources/overhead/summaries/statistics/).
The field is produced by the line's voltage (emfs.info, transmission page). UK and Indian grids alternate at 50 Hz, so the field reverses direction fifty times a second (US grid: 60 Hz).

Field points down near the ground: the ground behaves as a conductor and an electric field meets a conductor's surface at right angles (standard electrostatics, e.g. Griffiths, Introduction to Electrodynamics, 4th ed., sec. 2.5). A horizontal tube therefore lies almost along a line of equal voltage and gets almost no voltage between its ends; an upright tube spans the field. Simplified model, labelled on screen.

Fluorescent lamp: a glass tube of argon and mercury vapour; when current flows the gas is ionized and emits ultraviolet radiation; the phosphor coating absorbs the ultraviolet and fluoresces as visible light. Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Fluorescent lamp', https://www.britannica.com/technology/fluorescent-lamp

Art installation 'Field' by Richard Box, 2004, near Bristol UK: 1,301 tubes per the artist (Times Higher Education, 20 Feb 2004, https://www.timeshighereducation.com/node/49575), 'several thousand' per the University of Bristol press release (https://bristol.ac.uk/news/2004/360.html); the bulbs 'pick up the waste emission from the overhead power line'. Script says 'over a thousand', true for both.
